title: Iranian MP says Indian ships are exempt from Hormuz curbs, but must still pay fees
dek: A senior lawmaker named India, China, Iraq and Qatar as exempt from Iran's transit restrictions. New Delhi has not confirmed any arrangement, and US sanctions warnings cover any payments to Iran for passage.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
A senior Iranian lawmaker says ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar are exempt from Iran's restrictions on traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Indian and Chinese vessels still pay transit fees, according to reports of his remarks. India has not confirmed the arrangement. The Iranian government has not formally announced it either.

Ahmad Hayat-Moghaddam is deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament's national security and foreign policy committee. On Tuesday he told an Iranian news agency: "We have currently exempted four countries - India, China, Iraq and Qatar - from transit restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz." He said the decision was based on Iran's interests and its relations with those countries, reports said. Some outlets spell his name Amir Hayat Moghadam.

> "Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either." Ahmad Hayat-Moghaddam, according to one report

## What he said about India

According to reports, the lawmaker said India's exemption was meant to make it easier for Iran to import medicines from India, while China's was intended to secure Beijing's political support. Indian and Chinese ships continue to pay transit fees, while Qatari ships pass free of charge, one report said. It was not clear whether Iraqi ships pay.

The remarks come from a member of parliament, not from Iran's foreign ministry or the authority that runs the strait. None of the reports describes any formal notice to shipowners.

## The sanctions problem

Paying Iran for passage carries risks of its own. On 1 May, the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) warned that Iran's "toll" demands could take many forms. It listed cash, digital assets, swaps and "charitable" donations. OFAC said anyone who pays could face US sanctions, and that foreign firms could face secondary sanctions. It told maritime service providers to ask counterparties whether any safe-passage fee had been or would be paid. Indian shipowners, insurers and banks that deal with the US financial system fall within the scope of that warning.

## Why it matters for India

India's foreign ministry has not commented on the lawmaker's claim. After an Indian-flagged vessel, the MSV Al Jusufi, was attacked off Oman on Monday, killing one Indian sailor, the ministry called for "immediate de-escalation" and for "free and unimpeded navigation through international waterways". One report says that at least 15 Indian seafarers have been killed in attacks on ships since the war began on 28 February. Through all this, India's stated position has stayed the same: it wants dialogue and diplomacy.

A large share of the oil and gas India imports from the Gulf normally passes through the strait. Shipping through it has been badly disrupted since the war began, when US and Israeli strikes on Iran triggered Iranian retaliation.

## The wider picture

The claim comes during a tense week. US forces carried out what Washington called limited defensive strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island. Iran's Revolutionary Guards then claimed that four oil tankers had hit mines on a route they called prohibited and that they had seized two ships. Reports carried those claims, and they have not been independently verified. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has said the strait could reopen within two days of an agreement. Qatar is mediating between Tehran and Washington, and both sides say no deal has been reached.
